# ECON 0100 | Vignette E3 | Monopoly

::: solution

# Solutions

:::

*Answers and work are shown in the red blocks.*

*Vignettes are a certificate of the work done together in Recitation. Due in Recitation.*

Cauldron Co. is the only firm selling traditional cauldrons. It faces the whole market’s demand, $P = 70 - Q$, so its marginal revenue is $MR = 70 - 2Q$.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=60%}

### Q1 | Cauldron Co.

Initially, the Cauldron Co. has high fixed cost, and a low constant marginal cost of $MC = 10$.

a\) Graph and calculate the firm’s profit max quantity ($q^*$).

::: solution

Profit is largest where $MR = MC$: $70 - 2Q = 10$, so $q^* = 30$.

:::

b\) Graph and calculate the firm’s profit max price ($P^*$).

::: solution

Go up to demand at 30 cauldrons: $P^* = 70 - 30 = 40$.

:::

c\) Graph and calculate the firm’s maximal profit ($\pi^*$) if $ATC^* = 20$.

::: solution

$\pi^* = (P^* - ATC^*) \times q^* = (40 - 20) \times 30 = 600$ coins: the rectangle between the price and $ATC^*$, out to 30.

:::

d\) Graph and calculate the socially efficient quantity.

::: solution

Where demand crosses $MC$: $70 - Q = 10$, so $Q = 60$.

:::

e\) Graph and calculate the monopolist’s DWL.

::: solution

The triangle between demand and $MC$ from 30 to 60: $\frac{1}{2}(40 - 10)(60 - 30) = 450$ coins.

:::

:::

::: {.column width=40%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

### Q2 | Taxing The Cauldron Monopoly

To attempt to mitigate the issue of monopoly DWL, the Ministry of Magic decides taxes every cauldron 20 coins, raising Cauldron Co.’ marginal cost to: $MC = 30$.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=60%}

a\) Graph and calculate $q^*$ and $P^*$ after the new cost.

::: solution

$70 - 2Q = 30$, so $q^* = 20$. The price is $P^* = 70 - 20 = 50$.

:::

b\) Graph and calculate $\pi^*$ after the new cost if $ATC^* = 45$.

::: solution

$(50 - 45) \times 20 = 100$ coins, down from 600.

:::

c\) How much does price rise due to the tax?

::: solution

By 10, from 40 to 50: half of the 20-coin tax.

:::

d\) How much does the Ministry collect from this tax?

::: solution

$20 \times 20 = 400$ coins.

:::

e\) Calculate the DWL after the tax.

::: solution

A cauldron still costs 10 coins to make, so the lost trades are the ones between demand and 10, from 20 to 60: $\frac{1}{2}(50 - 10)(60 - 20) = 800$ coins, up from 450. The tax moves the quantity further from the efficient 60, so it makes the DWL larger, not smaller.

:::

:::

::: {.column width=40%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

### Q3 | Lump Sum Tax

Instead, a recent economics graduate proposes a lump sum tax of 600 coins on The Cauldron Co. instead of the tax on each cauldron. Its fixed costs rise while its marginal cost stays at $MC = 10$.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=60%}

a\) Graph and calculate $q^*$ and $P^*$ after the lump sum tax.

::: solution

Marginal cost is still 10, so nothing moves: $70 - 2Q = 10$ gives $q^* = 30$ and $P^* = 70 - 30 = 40$.

:::

b\) Graph and calculate $\pi^*$ after the lump sum tax if $ATC^* = 40$.

::: solution

$(40 - 40) \times 30 = 0$. The lump sum tax raises $ATC^*$ to the price, so it takes the whole profit of 600. The firm still just covers its costs, so it stays open.

:::

c\) How much does price rise due to the lump sum tax?

::: solution

Not at all. A lump sum tax is a fixed cost, and fixed costs do not change the profit-maximizing quantity or price.

:::

d\) Calculate the DWL after the lump sum tax.

::: solution

The quantity is still 30, so the DWL is still 450 coins.

:::

e\) How much does the Ministry collect under this tax.

::: solution

600 coins, against 400 from the tax on each cauldron.

:::

f\) Which tax is better for buyers?

::: solution

The lump sum tax. The price stays at 40 instead of rising to 50. It also collects more and adds no deadweight loss, but it does not reduce the monopoly’s DWL either.

:::

:::

::: {.column width=40%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

# ECON 0100 | Vignette E4 | Duopoly

<!-- Usage, 2026-11-19. Fall 2026 Vignette E4: The Cauldron Co. and a rival with the same costs (fixed cost 300, not stated; the profit part gives ATC* = 25; MC = 10) in the Vignette E3 market, P = 70 - Q. Best response q = 30 - q'/2, 20 each, price 30, profit 100 each; against the monopoly: 40 cauldrons instead of 30, price 30 instead of 40, DWL 200 instead of 450, total profit 200 instead of 600. The question text is copied from the handout by script; the red blocks and graph are Claude’s. The lump sum tax part of the first draft (each firm loses 100 and one leaves) was cut by Taylor on 2026-11-19. The Wandmaker’s Dilemma, the Vignette E4 draft of 2026-11-11, is in ../../E_Practice_Bank as Vignette_E4_wandmakers-dilemma_F26-draft (+_sols), and the Witching Hour version is there as Vignette_E4_witching-hour-duopoly_F26-draft. -->

Originally, Cauldron Co. makes substantial profits as the only seller of traditional cauldrons. This profit draws in a rival with the same costs: high fixed costs and a constant marginal cost of $MC = 10$. They sell into the same market, so $P = 70 - (q_C + q_R)$, where $q_C$ is The Cauldron Co.’s quantity and $q_R$ is its rival’s. The Cauldron Co.’s marginal revenue is $MR_C = 70 - 2q_C - q_R$. This market is symmetric.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=60%}

### Q1 | Two Cauldron Makers

a\) Find and graph both firms’ best responses.

::: solution

$MR_C = MC$: $70 - 2q_C - q_R = 10$, so $q_C = 30 - \frac{1}{2} q_R$. The rival’s is the mirror image, $q_R = 30 - \frac{1}{2} q_C$. Fixed costs do not appear: they do not change the cost of one more cauldron.

:::

b\) Calculate and graph the Nash equilibrium quantities.

::: solution

The market is symmetric, so $q = 30 - \frac{1}{2} q$ and each firm makes 20: the point where the two lines cross.

:::

c\) Calculate the Nash equilibrium price in this market.

::: solution

The market quantity is $20 + 20 = 40$, so $P = 70 - 40 = 30$.

:::

d\) Calculate each firm’s profit if $ATC^* = 25$.

::: solution

$(30 - 25) \times 20 = 100$ coins each.

:::

e\) How does this equilibrium compare to the monopoly equilibrium in Vignette E3?

::: solution

More cauldrons at a lower price: 40 at 30 coins instead of 30 at 40. The DWL falls from 450 to $\frac{1}{2}(30 - 10)(60 - 40) = 200$. Total profit falls from 600 to 200, because the price is lower and the fixed cost is paid twice.

:::

:::

::: {.column width=40%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::
